passages.title: Holidays with grandmother
passages.text: Odongo and Apiyo lived in the city with their father. They looked forward to the holidays. Not just because school was closed, but because they went to visit their grandmother. She lived in a fishing village near a large lake. Odongo and Apiyo were excited because it was time to visit their grandmother again. The night before, they packed their bags and got ready for the long journey to her village. They could not sleep and talked the whole night about the holiday.

question.q: What did Odongo and Apiyo do the night before the trip?
choices: They visited the fishing village
They packed their bags for the journey
They went fishing in the big lake
They said goodbye to their school friends
question.evidence: The night before, they packed their bags
question.explain: The paragraph says they packed their bags the night before the long journey.

passages.title: Chicken and Millipede
passages.text: Chicken and Millipede were friends. But they were always competing with each other. One day they decided to play football to see who the best player was. They went to the football field and started their game. Chicken was fast, but Millipede was faster. Chicken kicked far, but Millipede kicked further. Chicken started to feel grumpy.

question.q: Why did Chicken start to feel grumpy?
choices: Millipede was beating her at everything
The football field was far too muddy
Her friends would not let her play
She had hurt her foot kicking the ball
question.evidence: Chicken was fast, but Millipede was faster.
question.explain: Millipede was faster and kicked further, so Chicken was losing.

passages.title: Grandma's bananas
passages.text: Grandma's garden was wonderful, full of sorghum, millet, and cassava. But best of all were the bananas. Although Grandma had many grandchildren, I secretly knew that I was her favourite. She invited me often to her house. She also told me little secrets. But there was one secret she did not share with me: where she ripened bananas.

question.q: How does the girl telling the story feel about Grandma?
choices: Afraid of her strict rules
Bored by her long stories
Annoyed that she keeps secrets
Close to her and loved by her
question.evidence: I secretly knew that I was her favourite
question.explain: She visits often, hears secrets and feels like the favourite, so they are close.

passages.title: The happy revival
passages.text: For ages, Olokwango hill stood smiling at the middle of Kwere plains. From the two dimples on its side came springs which converged downhill to form a river. River Temu meandered silently across the Kwere plains. Its waters were a gift to the sheep and goats of the area as well as the deer that dwelt in the plains.

question.q: River Temu "meandered" across the plains. What does meandered mean?
choices: Rushed straight down in a flood
Dried up in the hot season
Flowed in a slow, winding path
Froze into a sheet of ice
question.evidence: River Temu meandered silently across the Kwere plains
question.explain: A river that meanders moves slowly and quietly, twisting and turning.

passages.title: The day I left home for the city
passages.text: The city bus was almost full, but more people were still pushing to get on. Some packed their luggage under the bus. Others put theirs on the racks inside. New passengers clutched their tickets as they looked for somewhere to sit in the crowded bus. Women with young children made them comfortable for the long journey.

question.q: What is this paragraph mostly about?
choices: A family packing their bags at home at night
People crowding onto a bus for a long trip
A driver fixing a broken bus by the road
Children playing games while waiting at a station
question.evidence: The city bus was almost full, but more people were still pushing to get on.
question.explain: Every sentence describes passengers getting on and settling into a crowded bus.

passages.title: Graca's dream
passages.text: Graca was about to be born in a small village in Mozambique. The country was poor and the people did not yet rule themselves. Children didn't have good schools and many couldn't read. Graca's mother dreamed of giving her children better opportunities. But without education there was little hope. Baby Graca would be the sixth child. But with this joyous event there was great sadness. Their beloved father was dying. He dreamed that his youngest daughter would go to a good school. He knew that education would give her opportunities he never had. His family promised to make their dad's dream come true.

question.q: What did Graca's family believe about school?
choices: It would give Graca a better life
It was only for the oldest child
It mattered less than work on the farm
It was too far away to reach
question.evidence: He knew that education would give her opportunities he never had.
question.explain: Her parents dreamed of school for her because education brings opportunities.

passages.title: Queen of Soweto: The Story of Basetsana Kumalo
passages.text: Basetsana Makgalemele was born in a township called Soweto. She was her parents' third daughter. They named her Basetsana, which means "girls". In Tswana culture, calling your daughter that means your next child will be a boy. This actually happened. Her parents' next child was a boy. Her parents, big sisters and younger brother all called her Bassie for short.

question.q: In Tswana culture, what does naming a daughter Basetsana mean?
choices: She will become a queen one day
She will be the last child born
The family will move to the city
The family's next child will be a boy
question.evidence: calling your daughter that means your next child will be a boy
question.explain: The paragraph explains the name means the next child will be a boy.

passages.title: Namoratunga
passages.text: Long time ago, in a Turkana village, people loved to dance the edonga dance. Every evening they gathered together and danced edonga. The whole region came to know of this village and its dancers. People from the nearby villages also came to dance edonga. A stranger heard of the famous village. He sent his messenger to go there before him.

question.q: What did the stranger do after he heard about the famous village?
choices: He came to teach them a new dance
He told the nearby villages to stay away
He sent a messenger there ahead of him
He built a house next to the dancers
question.evidence: He sent his messenger to go there before him.
question.explain: First the stranger heard of the village, then he sent his messenger ahead.

passages.title: Anansi and Vulture
passages.text: Anansi the Spider and Rabbit were friends. They lived in a peaceful village in the mountains. Rabbit owned a big farm with lots of vegetables and fruit. Even though Rabbit shared generously with his friend, Anansi was unhappy and jealous. So Anansi thought of a clever plan to take over Rabbit's farm. Soon Rabbit was left poor and homeless. Anansi was the proud owner of all Rabbit's land, vegetables, and fruit.

question.q: What kind of friend was Anansi to Rabbit?
choices: A loyal friend who shared his food
A jealous friend who tricked him
A shy friend who rarely visited
A helpful friend who worked his farm
question.evidence: Anansi was unhappy and jealous
question.explain: Anansi was jealous and used a plan to take everything Rabbit owned.

passages.title: Grandmother and the Smelly Girl
passages.text: Tasneem was a very beautiful girl and her grandmother was very kind. Her grandmother spent many hours making a handsome makgabe for Tasneem. Tasneem loved to wear that apron. The other girls in that place were jealous of Tasneem's makgabe. They thought that it would be better to get rid of it. But it is a difficult thing to take a person's clothes when that person is wearing them.

question.q: From the paragraph, what is a makgabe?
choices: A kind of apron
A kind of necklace
A kind of hat
A kind of basket
question.evidence: Tasneem loved to wear that apron.
question.explain: Right after the makgabe is mentioned, the paragraph calls it "that apron."

passages.title: Bonda and Devi
passages.text: "Again! Stack them up again, Bonda! I want to try knocking them down from a different angle!" Without hesitating for a moment, without even frowning, Bonda puts one battered box on top of the other for the fiftieth time. The high, shaky, cardboard tower is perfectly balanced, the way only Bonda knows how to build it.

question.q: What does the paragraph show about Bonda?
choices: He is tired of building towers
He is angry about the broken boxes
He wants a turn knocking them down
He is patient and glad to keep helping
question.evidence: Without hesitating for a moment, without even frowning
question.explain: Bonda rebuilds the tower for the fiftieth time without even frowning.

passages.title: Rupa's Vacation
passages.text: Rini, Neha and Rupa are three friends. Rini and Neha are twins and Rupa's mother is the elder sister of Rini and Neha, so Rini and Neha are actually Rupa's 'mausis'. But Rini and Neha are only one year older than Rupa and they are close friends. Rini and Neha live in Murshidabad a town in West Bengal. They go to a village school, Rupa lives in a big city Kolkata and goes to a school there. The friends would very much love to be together but cannot because of school.

question.q: Rini and Neha are Rupa's "mausis." From the paragraph, a mausi is
choices: your father's brother
your older cousin
your mother's sister
your school teacher
question.evidence: Rupa's mother is the elder sister of Rini and Neha
question.explain: Rini and Neha are sisters of Rupa's mother, so a mausi is a mother's sister.

passages.title: Jimmy Skunk's Black Coat
passages.text: Jimmy Skunk, as everybody knows, wears a striped suit, a suit of black and white. There was a time, long, long ago, when all the Skunk family wore black. Very handsome their coats were, too, a beautiful, glossy black. They were very, very proud of them and took the greatest care of them, brushing them carefully ever so many times a day.

source.name: Old Mother West Wind (Thornton W. Burgess, 1910)
source.author: Thornton W. Burgess

question.q: Long ago, what did the coats of all the Skunk family look like?
choices: Black and white
Shiny all black
Striped brown
Gray and white
question.evidence: all the Skunk family wore black
question.explain: Long ago all the Skunks wore glossy black coats, not stripes.

passages.title: The Great Race
passages.text: The Merry Little Breezes flew along, too, to see that the race was fair. Peter Rabbit went with great big jumps. Whenever he came to a little bush he jumped right over it, for Peter Rabbit's legs are long and meant for jumping. Billy Mink is so slim that he slipped between the bushes and through the long grass like a little brown streak. Reddy Fox, who is bigger than either Peter Rabbit or Billy Mink, had no trouble in keeping up with them. Not one of them noticed that Spotty the Turtle was hanging fast to the end of Reddy's tail.

source.name: Old Mother West Wind (Thornton W. Burgess, 1910)
source.author: Thornton W. Burgess

question.q: How was slow Spotty the Turtle able to keep up with the racers?
choices: He was riding along on Reddy Fox's tail
He took a shortcut through the long grass
The Merry Little Breezes carried him
He jumped over the bushes like Peter
question.evidence: Spotty the Turtle was hanging fast to the end of Reddy's tail
question.explain: Spotty held on to Reddy's tail, so Reddy carried him along.

passages.title: Flies for Grandfather Frog
passages.text: Old Grandfather Frog sat on his big green lily pad blinking in the sun. It was very still, very, very still indeed. Suddenly out of the brown bulrushes burst the Merry Little Breezes and surrounded old Grandfather Frog. And every one of them had brought to him a fat, foolish, green fly.

source.name: Mother West Wind's Children (Thornton W. Burgess, 1911)
source.author: Thornton W. Burgess

question.q: What broke the stillness around Grandfather Frog?
choices: A fat green fly buzzed past his nose
Grandfather Frog dove into the water
A loud splash came from the bulrushes
The Merry Little Breezes burst in
question.evidence: Suddenly out of the brown bulrushes burst the Merry Little Breezes
question.explain: After the quiet, the Merry Little Breezes suddenly burst out of the bulrushes.

passages.title: Sammy Jay's Blue Coat
passages.text: Sammy Jay has a very fine coat, a very beautiful coat. Everybody knows that. In fact, Sammy's coat has long been the envy of a great many of his neighbors in the Green Forest. Some of them, you know, have very modest coats. They are not beautiful at all. And yet the owners of some of these plain coats are among the most honest and hard-working of all the little people who live in the Green Forest. They find it hard, very hard indeed, to understand why such a scamp and mischiefmaker as Sammy Jay should be given such a wonderful blue coat with white trimmings.

source.name: Mother West Wind 'Why' Stories (Thornton W. Burgess, 1915)
source.author: Thornton W. Burgess

question.q: What puzzles some of Sammy Jay's neighbors?
choices: Why Sammy Jay works so much harder than they do
Why their own coats are so colorful
Why a mischief-maker has such a fine coat
Why Sammy Jay never leaves the forest
question.evidence: They find it hard, very hard indeed, to understand why such a scamp and mischiefmaker as Sammy Jay should be given such a wonderful blue coat
question.explain: Honest, hard-working neighbors wonder why a scamp gets the beautiful coat.

passages.title: Watching Flitter the Bat
passages.text: Flitter the Bat made Peter Rabbit's head dizzy. Peter couldn't help watching him. He just had to. It seemed so wonderful that Flitter could really fly, that whenever he saw him, Peter had to stop and watch. And then, as he saw Flitter twist and turn, fly high, fly low, and go round and round, Peter's head would begin to swim and grow dizzy, and he wondered and wondered how it was that Flitter himself didn't grow dizzy.

source.name: Mother West Wind 'Why' Stories (Thornton W. Burgess, 1915)
source.author: Thornton W. Burgess

question.q: What is this paragraph mostly about?
choices: Flitter teaching Peter how to fly
Peter getting dizzy watching Flitter fly
Peter chasing Flitter all around the Smiling Pool
Flitter getting dizzy from flying
question.evidence: Peter's head would begin to swim and grow dizzy
question.explain: Peter cannot stop watching Flitter twist and turn, and it makes him dizzy.

passages.title: Thinking of Winter
passages.text: Peter Rabbit had been making fun of Happy Jack Squirrel because Happy Jack said that he had too much to do to stop and play that morning. Here it was summer, and winter was a long way off. What was summer for if not to play in and have a good time? Yet Happy Jack was already thinking of winter and was hunting for a new storehouse so as to have it ready when the time to fill it with nuts should come. It was much better to play and take sun-naps among the buttercups and daisies and just have a good time all day long.

source.name: Mother West Wind 'How' Stories (Thornton W. Burgess, 1916)
source.author: Thornton W. Burgess

question.q: Who is planning ahead in this paragraph, and how?
choices: Happy Jack, by readying a storehouse
Peter, by saving buttercups for winter
Peter, by taking sun-naps every day
Happy Jack, by playing all summer long
question.evidence: Yet Happy Jack was already thinking of winter
question.explain: Happy Jack is hunting for a storehouse now so it is ready for winter nuts.

passages.title: Carol the Meadow Lark
passages.text: Somehow Peter never before had realized how handsome Carol the Meadow Lark was. As he faced Peter, the latter saw a beautiful yellow throat and waistcoat, with a broad black crescent on his breast. There was a yellow line above each eye. His back was of brown with black markings. His sides were whitish, with spats and streaks of black. The outer edges of his tail were white. Altogether he was really handsome, far handsomer than one would suspect, seeing him at a distance.

source.name: The Burgess Bird Book for Children (Thornton W. Burgess, 1919)
source.author: Thornton W. Burgess

question.q: What mark did Carol the Meadow Lark have on his breast?
choices: A round bright red spot
A long thin white stripe
A yellow ring
A black crescent shape
question.evidence: a broad black crescent on his breast
question.explain: The paragraph says he had a broad black crescent on his breast.

passages.title: Jimmy Skunk on the Hunt
passages.text: Jimmy Skunk raised himself on his hind-legs a little to see just where Bubbling Bob dropped down in the grass. Then Jimmy began to move in that direction. Suddenly Peter understood. He remembered that Bubbling Bob's nest is always on the ground. It was his eggs that Jimmy Skunk was looking for.

source.name: The Burgess Bird Book for Children (Thornton W. Burgess, 1919)
source.author: Thornton W. Burgess

question.q: Why was Jimmy Skunk moving toward the spot where Bubbling Bob landed?
choices: He wanted to listen to Bubbling Bob's song
He was hiding from Peter Rabbit
He was looking for Bubbling Bob's eggs
He was going home to his own nest
question.evidence: It was his eggs that Jimmy Skunk was looking for.
question.explain: Bubbling Bob's nest is on the ground, and Jimmy wanted the eggs.

passages.title: True Seals
passages.text: The true Seals are short-necked, thick-bodied, and have rather round heads with no visible ears. The Walrus and Sea Lions can turn their hind flippers forward to use as feet on land, but this the true Seals cannot do. Therefore they are more clumsy out of water. Their front flippers are covered with hair.

source.name: The Burgess Animal Book for Children (Thornton W. Burgess, 1920)
source.author: Thornton W. Burgess

question.q: Why are true Seals more clumsy out of water?
choices: Their front flippers are covered with thick hair
They cannot turn their hind flippers forward
Their necks are too long and thin
They have no ears to hear danger
question.evidence: Therefore they are more clumsy out of water
question.explain: Walruses and Sea Lions use turned-forward hind flippers as feet; true Seals cannot.

passages.title: A Wonderful Jump
passages.text: Nimbleheels hopped down from the log on which he had been sitting and at once shot into the air in such a high, long, beautiful jump that everybody exclaimed. This way and that way he went in great leaps. It was truly wonderful.

source.name: The Burgess Animal Book for Children (Thornton W. Burgess, 1920)
source.author: Thornton W. Burgess

question.q: What is Nimbleheels especially good at?
choices: Leaping high and far
Climbing very tall trees
Digging deep holes
Swimming fast
question.evidence: such a high, long, beautiful jump that everybody exclaimed
question.explain: Everybody exclaimed at his great leaps, so he is a fine jumper.

passages.title: William Tell
passages.text: William Tell's home was among the mountains, and he was a famous hunter. No one in all the land could shoot with bow and arrow so well as he. Gessler knew this, and so he thought of a cruel plan to make the hunter's own skill bring him to grief. He ordered that Tell's little boy should be made to stand up in the public square with an apple on his head; and then he bade Tell shoot the apple with one of his arrows.

question.q: Why was Gessler's plan so cruel?
choices: Tell had never used a bow before
The apple was poisoned with something
The square was too far for any arrow
Tell might hit his own son by mistake
question.evidence: Tell's little boy should be made to stand up in the public square with an apple on his head
question.explain: If Tell missed the apple, the arrow could hit his little boy.

passages.title: The Butter Lion
passages.text: On the kitchen table there was a large square lump of yellow butter. Two hundred pounds the lump weighed, and it had just come in, fresh and clean, from the dairy on the mountain. With a kitchen knife in his hand, Antonio began to cut and carve this butter. In a few minutes he had molded it into the shape of a crouching lion; and all the servants crowded around to see it.

question.q: Antonio made "a crouching lion." What does crouching mean?
choices: Roaring with its mouth open
Running fast across a field
Bent low, close to the ground
Sleeping curled up in a ball
question.evidence: he had molded it into the shape of a crouching lion
question.explain: A crouching animal bends its legs and stays low to the ground.

passages.title: Alexander and Bucephalus
passages.text: Everybody expected to see the boy killed outright. But he kept his place, and let the horse run as fast as he would. By and by, when Bucephalus had become tired, Alexander reined him in, and rode back to the place where his father was standing.

question.q: What did Alexander do once Bucephalus had become tired?
choices: He jumped down and let the tired horse go free
He reined him in and rode back to his father
He gave the horse a long drink of water
He kept riding faster until night came
question.evidence: when Bucephalus had become tired, Alexander reined him in
question.explain: First the horse ran until tired; then Alexander reined him in and rode back.

passages.title: Prince Gautama
passages.text: In the Far East there was once a prince whose name was Gautama. He lived in a splendid palace where there was everything that could give delight. It was the wish of his father and mother that every day of his life should be a day of perfect happiness.

question.q: What did Gautama's father and mother wish for him?
choices: That every day would be perfectly happy
That he would become a great soldier
That he would travel far across the world
That he would leave the palace soon
question.evidence: every day of his life should be a day of perfect happiness
question.explain: His parents wished every day of his life to be perfectly happy.

passages.title: St. Francis
passages.text: The man of whom I am now going to tell you was famous, not for his wealth or his power or his deeds in war, but for his great gentleness. He lived more than seven hundred years ago in a quaint little town of Italy. His name was Francis, and because of his goodness, all men now call him St. Francis.

question.q: Why was Francis famous, according to the paragraph?
choices: For his wealth and great power
For his brave deeds in war
For building a little Italian town
For being so gentle and good
question.evidence: famous, not for his wealth or his power or his deeds in war, but for his great gentleness
question.explain: He was famous for his gentleness and goodness, not wealth, power or war.

passages.title: Zeuxis and the Cherries
passages.text: Some time after this, Zeuxis painted another wonderful picture. It was that of a boy carrying a basket of ripe red cherries. When he hung this painting outside of his door, some birds flew down and tried to carry the cherries away.

question.q: What does the birds' visit show about the painting?
choices: The painting was hung too low
The birds liked the boy
The cherries looked very real
The colors were fading quickly
question.evidence: some birds flew down and tried to carry the cherries away
question.explain: The birds were fooled into thinking the painted cherries were real fruit.

passages.title: The Box of Treasure
passages.text: "Well, it is this way," answered the man: "I bought a piece of ground from this neighbor of mine, and paid him a fair price for it. Yesterday, when I was digging in it, I found a box full of gold and jewels. This treasure does not belong to me, for I bought only the ground; but when I offered it to my neighbor he refused it."

question.q: Why does the man say the treasure does not belong to him?
choices: He found it while digging on his neighbor's land
He bought only the ground, not the box
The box was too heavy to carry home
The jewels turned out to be fake
question.evidence: This treasure does not belong to me, for I bought only the ground
question.explain: He paid for the land only, so he feels the treasure is not his.

passages.title: The Coming Rain
passages.text: Rain forms in the distance like a dim curtain extending clear across the sky. The sheet of water advances rapidly; it would beat the fastest racing horse. It is coming, it has come. Violent flashes of lightning furrow it, thunder roars in its depths.

source.name: The Story-Book of Science (Jean-Henri Fabre, 1917)
source.author: Jean-Henri Fabre
source.note: Paragraph from the book. Translated by Florence Constable Bicknell.

question.q: Flashes of lightning "furrow" the rain. What does furrow mean here?
choices: Cut lines across it
Make it grow warmer
Push it backward
Turn it into snow
question.evidence: Violent flashes of lightning furrow it
question.explain: A furrow is a long line cut into something, like a plow line in a field.

passages.title: Counting Tree Rings
passages.text: "I must tell you," continued Uncle Paul, "that those circles are called annual layers. Why annual, if you please? Because one is formed every year; one only, understand, neither more nor less. The learned who spend their lives studying plants, and who are called botanists, tell us that no doubt is possible on that point. From the moment the little tree springs from the seed to the time when the old tree dies, every year there is formed a ring, a layer of wood. This understood, let us count the layers of our pear-tree."

source.name: The Story-Book of Science (Jean-Henri Fabre, 1917)
source.author: Jean-Henri Fabre
source.note: Paragraph from the book. Translated by Florence Constable Bicknell.

question.q: How often does a tree form an annual layer?
choices: Two layers every year
One layer every month
One layer after every big rainstorm
Exactly one each year
question.evidence: every year there is formed a ring, a layer of wood
question.explain: Uncle Paul says one layer forms every year, neither more nor less.

passages.title: The Bee's Harvest
passages.text: The bee enters a flower, plunges to the bottom of the corolla a long and flexible trunk, a kind of tongue that laps the sweet liquor. Droplet by droplet, drawn from this flower and that, the crop is filled. The bee at the same time nibbles a few grains of pollen. Moreover, it proposes to carry a good load of it to the hive. It has special utensils for this work: first, the down of its body, then the brushes and baskets that its legs supply. The down and the brushes are used for harvesting; the baskets for carrying.

source.name: The Story-Book of Science (Jean-Henri Fabre, 1917)
source.author: Jean-Henri Fabre
source.note: Paragraph from the book. Translated by Florence Constable Bicknell.

question.q: What does the bee use the baskets on its legs for?
choices: For harvesting the pollen
For lapping up sweet liquid
For carrying pollen loads
For storing wax in the hive
question.evidence: the baskets for carrying
question.explain: The down and brushes harvest the pollen; the baskets carry it.

passages.title: An Evening Story
passages.text: In the evening Mother Ambroisine, her large round spectacles on her nose, was knitting stockings. On her knees the cat slept and mingled its purring with the tick-tack of the needles. The children were waiting for the story of the spider. Their uncle began.

source.name: The Story-Book of Science (Jean-Henri Fabre, 1917)
source.author: Jean-Henri Fabre
source.note: Paragraph from the book. Translated by Florence Constable Bicknell.

question.q: What scene does this paragraph describe?
choices: A busy morning at the town market
A quiet evening before a story
A noisy party in the kitchen
A stormy night with no lights
question.evidence: The children were waiting for the story of the spider.
question.explain: It is a calm evening, with knitting and a purring cat, as the children wait for a story.

passages.title: Telling History Fairly
passages.text: Few things in human life are either entirely good or entirely bad. Few things are either black or white. It is the duty of the honest chronicler to give a true account of all the good and bad sides of every historical event. It is very difficult to do this because we all have our personal likes and dislikes. But we ought to try and be as fair as we can be, and must not allow our prejudices to influence us too much.

source.name: The Story of Mankind (Hendrik Willem van Loon, 1921)
source.author: Hendrik Willem van Loon

question.q: What is the main point of this paragraph?
choices: Historians should try to tell both sides
History is mostly about bad events
Only the good events should ever be written down
Personal likes make history more fun
question.evidence: give a true account of all the good and bad sides of every historical event
question.explain: The writer says a historian must show good and bad sides and be fair.

passages.title: Dates Play Tricks
passages.text: Dates are a very useful invention. We could not do without them but unless we are very careful, they will play tricks with us. They are apt to make history too precise. For example, when I talk of the point-of-view of mediaeval man, I do not mean that on the 31st of December of the year 476, suddenly all the people of Europe said, "Ah, now the Roman Empire has come to an end and we are living in the Middle Ages. How interesting!"

source.name: The Story of Mankind (Hendrik Willem van Loon, 1921)
source.author: Hendrik Willem van Loon

question.q: What trick can dates play on us?
choices: They make history seem far too long
They make old events seem very recent
They make us forget the names of important people
They make changes seem to happen in one day
question.evidence: They are apt to make history too precise.
question.explain: People did not suddenly enter the Middle Ages on one date, though dates make it seem so.
